html:
The Uzbek khanates were the states of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand that ruled the oases of Central Asia from about 1500 until the Russian Revolution. The chart groups them into one bar.

They began when Muhammad Shaybani, a descendant of Genghis Khan, led Uzbek nomads south from the steppe and took the Timurid cities: Samarkand, Bukhara, Herat and Tashkent, between 1500 and 1507. He drove the Timurid prince Babur out of Central Asia. Shaybani was killed in 1510 fighting the new Safavid shah of Iran, and the border between Shia Iran and the Sunni Uzbeks hardened.

The three states:

  • Bukhara: the strongest, capital of the khanate from the 1500s; from 1785 the Manghit dynasty ruled it as an emirate.
  • Khiva, in the old land of Khwarazm on the lower Oxus; known for its slave market, fed by raids on Iranians and Russians.
  • Kokand, in the Ferghana valley, which broke away from Bukhara in the 1700s.

Trade along the old Silk Road routes declined as sea trade grew, and the khanates were often at war with one another and with Iran.

In the 1800s they lay between the Russian and British empires. Russia moved first. After Russia took Tashkent in 1865, Bukhara became a protectorate in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, when the slave market was closed. Kokand was annexed outright in 1876. In 1920 the Red Army overthrew the emir of Bukhara and the khan of Khiva, and the lands were folded into Soviet rule.
sum: The Uzbek khanates were the states of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand that ruled the oases of Central Asia from about 1500 until the Russian Revolution. The chart groups them into one bar.
